1. These are the marks of the rational soul. It sees itself, examines itself, and makes itself whatever it chooses to be. It enjoys the fruit it bears itself—whereas the fruits of plants, and whatever in animals corresponds to fruit, are enjoyed by others. It reaches its own goal wherever the limit of life is set. It is not like a dance or a play or anything of that kind, where the whole performance is left incomplete if something cuts it short. In every part, and wherever it is stopped, it makes what it set out to do full and complete, so that it can say: I have what is my own. Further, it travels through the whole universe and the empty space around it, and surveys its shape. It reaches out into the endlessness of time, and grasps and understands the periodic renewal of all things. It understands that those who come after us will see nothing new, and that those who came before us saw nothing more. In a way, a person of forty, if he has any understanding at all, has seen everything that has been and everything that will be, because all things are so uniform. This too is a mark of the rational soul: love of one's neighbor, truthfulness and modesty, and valuing nothing more than itself—which is also a mark of law. So right reason and the reason of justice do not differ at all.

2. You will think little of delightful singing, of dancing, and of the pancratium—the all-in fighting contest—if you break the melody down into its separate notes and ask yourself of each one, "Is this what overpowers me?" You will be too ashamed to admit it. Do the same with dancing, at each movement and each pose; and the same with the pancratium. In everything, then, except virtue and the acts that come from virtue, remember to go to the separate parts, and by dividing things in this way come to think little of them. Apply the same method to your whole life too.

3. What a soul that is which is ready, if at any moment it must be separated from the body, to be extinguished, or scattered, or to go on existing! But this readiness must come from a person's own judgment, not from mere obstinacy, as with the Christians. It must be thought through and dignified, and such that it could persuade someone else, without any theatrical display.
4. Have I done something for the common good? Then I have had my reward. Keep this always before your mind, and never stop doing such good.
5. What is your craft? To be good. And how is this done well, except by means of general principles—some about the nature of the universe, and others about how a human being is properly made?

6. At first, tragedies were put on the stage to remind people of the things that happen to them: that it is according to nature for things to happen this way, and that if what is shown on the stage delights you, you should not be distressed by what happens on the larger stage. For you see that these things must turn out this way, and that even those who cry out "O Cithaeron!" have to bear them. And the dramatists do say some things well, especially this: "If the gods neglect me and my children, this too has its reason." And again: "We must not chafe and fret at what happens." And: "Reap life's harvest like the ripe ear of wheat." And other things of the same kind. After tragedy came the Old Comedy. It spoke with the frankness of a teacher, and its very bluntness was useful in reminding people to beware of arrogance; for this purpose Diogenes, too, used to borrow from these writers. But as for the Middle Comedy that came next, consider what it was; and then consider for what purpose the New Comedy was brought in, which little by little sank into mere skill at imitation. Everyone knows that even these writers say some good things. But the whole design of this kind of poetry and drama—what is it aiming at?
7. How plain it is that no other condition of life is so well suited to philosophy as the one you happen to be in now!

8. A branch cut off from the branch next to it is necessarily cut off from the whole tree as well. In the same way, a person separated from another person has fallen away from the whole community. A branch is cut off by someone else. But a person separates himself from his neighbor by his own act, when he hates him and turns away from him; and he does not realize that he has at the same time cut himself off from the whole body of society. Yet Zeus, who founded this community, has certainly given us this privilege: it is in our power to grow back onto what is next to us, and to become once more a part that helps make up the whole. But if this kind of separation happens often, it becomes hard for the part that breaks away to be united again and restored to what it was. In short, the branch that grew together with the tree from the start, and has always shared one life with it, is not like a branch that was cut off and then grafted back on. The grafted branch is something like what gardeners mean when they say that it grows along with the rest of the tree, but is not of one mind with it.

9. When you are going forward in keeping with right reason, those who try to stand in your way will not be able to turn you aside from acting rightly. So do not let them drive you from your kindly feeling toward them either. Guard both equally: not only steadiness in judgment and action, but also gentleness toward those who try to hinder you or trouble you in any other way. For it is a weakness to resent them, just as it is a weakness to be turned from your course of action and to give in out of fear. Both are deserters from their post alike: the one who gives in out of fear, and the one who becomes estranged from someone who is by nature his kinsman and friend.

10. No nature is inferior to art, for the arts imitate the natures of things. If this is so, then the nature that is the most perfect of all natures, and the one that contains them all, cannot fall short of the skill of art. Now all the arts make the lesser things for the sake of the higher; so the nature of the universe does this too. And this is where justice has its origin, and the other virtues have their foundation in justice. For justice will not be kept if we care about the in-between things that are neither good nor bad, or if we are easily deceived, careless and changeable.

11. If the things whose pursuit or avoidance disturbs you do not come to you, still, in a way, it is you who go to them. So let your judgment about them be at rest, and they will stay quiet, and you will not be seen chasing after them or running from them.

12. The soul keeps its shape as a sphere when it neither reaches out toward anything, nor shrinks inward, nor scatters, nor sinks down, but is lit by the light by which it sees the truth—the truth of all things and the truth within itself.

13. Suppose someone despises me. That is his concern. My concern is not to be found doing or saying anything that deserves contempt. Will someone hate me? That is his concern. But I will be gentle and kind toward everyone, and ready to show even that person his mistake—not reproachfully, nor as if showing off my patience, but nobly and honestly, like the great Phocion, unless he was only pretending. For that is how one ought to be within: a person should be seen by the gods neither discontented about anything nor complaining. For what is bad for you, if you are now doing what suits your own nature, and are content with what at this moment suits the nature of the universe—you, a human being placed at your post so that the common good may be achieved in one way or another?
14. People despise one another and flatter one another; they want to rise above one another, and they grovel before one another.

15. How rotten and false is the person who says, "I have decided to deal fairly with you!" What are you doing, man? There is no need to announce this. It will soon show itself in what you do. Your very voice ought to declare it, as plainly as if it were written on your forehead. Whatever a person's character is, it shows at once in his eyes, just as someone who is loved reads everything at once in the eyes of those who love him. The honest, good person ought to be exactly like someone who smells strongly, so that anyone who comes near him must notice it at once, whether he wants to or not. But a show of simplicity is like a crooked stick. Nothing is more shameful than the friendship of a wolf—false friendship. Avoid this above all. The good, the simple and the kind show all this in their eyes, and there is no mistaking it.

16. The power to live in the best way lies in the soul, if it is indifferent to things that are indifferent—that is, to things that are neither good nor bad. And it will be indifferent to them if it looks at each of these things both separately and as a whole, and if it remembers that none of them produces in us an opinion about itself, and none of them comes to us. They stay where they are, unmoving; it is we who produce the judgments about them and, so to speak, write them in ourselves. It is in our power not to write them; and if such judgments have slipped into our minds without our noticing, it is in our power to wipe them out. And it will be indifferent if we remember, too, that this care will be needed only for a short time, and then life will be over. Besides, what is so hard about doing this? If these things are in keeping with nature, take pleasure in them, and they will be easy for you. But if they are against nature, look for what suits your own nature and press on toward it, even if it brings you no fame; for everyone is allowed to seek his own good.
17. Consider where each thing has come from, what it is made of, what it changes into, what it will be like once it has changed, and that it will come to no harm.

18. If someone has wronged you, consider first: what is my relation to other people? We are made for one another; and, in another respect, I was made to be set over them, as a ram over the flock or a bull over the herd. But go back to first principles, and start from this: if all things are not mere atoms, then it is nature that orders all things. If that is so, the lower things exist for the sake of the higher, and the higher for the sake of one another. Second, consider what sort of people they are at table, in bed, and so on; and above all, what compulsions their opinions put them under; and as for their acts, consider with what pride they do what they do. Third, if they are doing right, we ought not to be displeased. If they are not doing right, it is plain that they do wrong against their will and out of ignorance. For just as every soul is deprived of the truth against its will, so too it is deprived against its will of the power to treat each person as he deserves. That is why people are pained when they are called unjust, ungrateful, greedy—in a word, wrongdoers toward their neighbors. Fourth, consider that you yourself do many things wrong, and that you are a human being like the others. Even if you keep from certain faults, you still have the tendency to commit them, though you keep from them out of cowardice, or concern for your reputation, or some other such petty motive. Fifth, consider that you do not even know for certain whether they are doing wrong, for many things are done with some circumstance in view. In short, a person has to learn a great deal before he can judge another person's acts correctly. Sixth, when you are deeply resentful or upset, consider that human life lasts only a moment, and after a short while we are all laid out dead. Seventh, it is not people's acts that disturb us, since those acts are rooted in their own ruling faculties; it is our own opinions that disturb us. So take away these opinions: resolve to let go of your judgment that the act is something terrible, and your anger is gone. How, then, shall I take away these opinions? By reflecting that no wrong act of another person brings shame on you. For unless what is shameful is the only thing that is bad, you too must inevitably do many wrongs, and become a robber and everything else. Eighth, consider how much more pain we suffer from the anger and resentment such acts cause us than from the acts themselves that we are angry and resentful about. Ninth, consider that a kindly disposition is invincible, if it is genuine and not a forced smile or an act. For what can even the most violent person do to you if you go on being kind to him, and, when the chance comes, gently advise him and calmly set him right at the very moment he is trying to harm you? Say to him: "No, my child; we were made by nature for something else. I shall certainly not be harmed; it is you who are harming yourself, my child." And show him, gently and tactfully and by general principles, that this is so, and that not even bees behave as he does, nor any animals that nature has made to live in herds. You must do this without any hidden meaning and without reproach, but with affection and with no bitterness in your soul; not as if you were lecturing him, nor so that some bystander may admire you, but either when he is alone, and if others are present . . . Remember these nine rules as if you had received them as a gift from the Muses, and begin at last to be a human being while you are still alive. But you must avoid flattering people just as much as resenting them, for both set us against others and lead to harm. And when anger stirs, keep this truth at hand: to be carried away by passion is not manly. Gentleness and mildness, just as they are more in keeping with human nature, are also more manly. Whoever has these qualities has strength, nerve and courage—not the person who is given to fits of passion and discontent. For the closer a mind comes to freedom from passion, the closer it comes to strength. And just as feeling pain is a sign of weakness, so is anger. For whoever gives in to pain and whoever gives in to anger are both wounded, and both have surrendered. And if you like, accept a tenth gift too, from Apollo, the leader of the Muses: to expect bad people not to do wrong is madness, for whoever expects this wants the impossible. But to let them behave like this toward others, and expect them not to wrong you, is unreasonable and tyrannical.

19. There are four chief ways in which the ruling faculty goes astray. Be constantly on guard against them, and when you catch them, wipe them out, saying each time: "This thought is not necessary." "This one tends to break the bonds of community." "What you are about to say does not come from your real thoughts"—and you should count it among the most absurd things for a person not to speak from his real thoughts. The fourth is when you reproach yourself for anything. For this shows that the more divine part in you has been overpowered and has given way to the less honorable and perishable part, the body, and to its coarse pleasures.

20. The airy part of you, and all the fiery parts mixed in you, tend upward by nature; yet in obedience to the ordering of the universe they are held down here in the compound mass of the body. And the whole of the earthy part in you, and the watery part, though they tend downward, are still raised up and hold a position that is not natural to them. In this way even the elements obey the whole: once they have been set in any place, they are forced to stay there until the whole sounds the signal for them to break up again. Is it not strange, then, that only your intelligent part should be disobedient and discontented with its place? And yet nothing is forced on it except what is in keeping with its nature. Still it does not submit, but is carried the opposite way. For the impulse toward injustice, self-indulgence, anger, grief and fear is nothing but the act of one who is turning away from nature. And when the ruling faculty is discontented with anything that happens, it too deserts its post. For it was made for piety and reverence toward the gods no less than for justice. These qualities, too, come under the general heading of contentment with the way things are ordered; and indeed they come before acts of justice.

21. Someone who does not have one aim in life, always the same, cannot be one and the same person all through his life. But what I have said is not enough unless I add what that aim ought to be. People do not all hold the same opinion about everything that most of them regard, in one way or another, as good; they agree only about certain things, namely the things that concern the common interest. In the same way, we ought to set ourselves an aim that is shared and civic—one that serves the community. For whoever directs all his own efforts toward this aim will make all his acts consistent, and so will always be the same.
22. Think of the country mouse and the town mouse, and of the town mouse's alarm and panic.
23. Socrates used to call the opinions of the many "Lamiae"—bogeys to frighten children.
24. The Lacedaemonians, at their public shows, used to set out seats in the shade for strangers, but sat down anywhere themselves.

25. Socrates excused himself to Perdiccas for not going to visit him, saying: "It is because I do not want to perish by the worst of all ends"—that is, to receive a favor and then be unable to return it.
26. In the writings of the Ephesians there was this rule: to keep constantly in mind one or another of the people of old who practiced virtue.

27. The Pythagoreans tell us to look at the sky in the morning, so that we are reminded of those bodies that always do the same things and do their work in the same way, and are reminded too of their purity and their nakedness. For no star wears a veil.

28. Think what kind of man Socrates was when he wrapped himself in an animal skin, after Xanthippe had taken his cloak and gone out; and what Socrates said to his friends who were ashamed of him and drew back from him when they saw him dressed like that.
29. In writing and in reading you will not be able to lay down rules for others until you have first learned to follow rules yourself. Much more is this true in life.
30. You are a slave: free speech is not for you.
31. As Homer says in the Odyssey: "And my heart laughed within me."
32. As Hesiod says in the Works and Days: "And they will curse virtue, speaking harsh words."
33. To look for a fig in winter is the act of a madman; and the person who looks for his child when that is no longer allowed is just like him. So Epictetus says.

34. When a person kisses his child, said Epictetus, he should whisper to himself: "Tomorrow, perhaps, you will die." "But those are words of ill omen." "No word is ill-omened," said Epictetus, "that speaks of any work of nature. Or if it is, then it is also ill-omened to speak of ears of grain being harvested."
35. The unripe grape, the ripe bunch, the dried grape: all are changes, not into nothing, but into something that does not yet exist. So Epictetus says.
36. No one can rob us of our free will, as Epictetus says.

37. Epictetus also said that a person must find an art, a set of rules, for giving assent. As for his impulses, he must take care that they take account of circumstances, that they serve the common good, and that they take account of the worth of their object. He should keep away from sensual desire altogether; and he should feel aversion toward none of the things that are not in our power.
38. So, he said, the dispute is not about some ordinary matter, but about whether we are to be mad or not.

39. Socrates used to say: "What do you want: the souls of rational beings, or of irrational ones?" "Of rational beings." "Rational beings of what kind: sound or unsound?" "Sound." "Then why do you not seek them?" "Because we have them." "Then why do you fight and quarrel?"
